# MarathiGPT
Status: complete
One-liner: A 54M-parameter GPT pretrained from scratch on Marathi with a custom tokenizer that's 4.8x more token-efficient than GPT-4 on the language.

Stack: PyTorch, SentencePiece, transformer pretraining
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Marathi-GPT

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
For Indic languages the binding constraint usually isn't model capacity, it's tokenization. GPT-4's tokenizer shreds Devanagari into fragments, so the same Marathi sentence costs several times more tokens than its English equivalent — which means worse context utilization, higher inference cost, and less semantic signal per token during training. So the project started at the tokenizer: a custom 32k SentencePiece vocabulary trained on Marathi, achieving 4.8x better token efficiency than GPT-4 on the same text. The transformer was then pretrained from scratch on top of it, at 54M parameters, with 22.9M (nano) and 42.1M (small) variants to see how the efficiency gain interacts with scale. Small models by design — the point was to demonstrate the tokenizer thesis end-to-end on a single consumer GPU, not to compete with anything.


## Metrics
- Token efficiency vs GPT-4 on Marathi: 4.8x
- Model sizes trained: 22.9M / 42.1M / 54M

## Anticipated questions
Q: Why build the tokenizer instead of fine-tuning an existing model?
A: Fine-tuning inherits the tokenizer, and the tokenizer is the actual bottleneck. You can't fine-tune your way out of spending 5x the tokens to say the same sentence.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-08-07T13:10:04Z
- GitHub description: GPT pretrained from scratch on Marathi — custom 32k SentencePiece tokenizer (4.8x fewer tokens than GPT-4's on Marathi), full corpus → cleaning → tokenizer → training → eval pipeline, trained on a single RTX 5070 (12GB)

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 123941

## README
# MarathiGPT

A GPT-style language model pretrained from scratch on Marathi text, nanoGPT-style
(architecture + training loop written from first principles, no fine-tuned base model).

Portfolio project: full pretraining stack — corpus collection, cleaning, a custom
tokenizer, model, training loop, and evaluation — for a low-resource Indian language,
trained on a single consumer GPU (RTX 5070, 12GB).

See [marathi-gpt-project-plan.md](marathi-gpt-project-plan.md) for the full blueprint.

## Status

Work in progress. Built phase by phase:

- [x] Phase 1 — Repo scaffold
- [x] Phase 2 — Data download
- [x] Phase 3 — Cleaning pipeline
- [x] Phase 4 — Tokenizer
- [x] Phase 5 — Pre-tokenization
- [x] Phase 6 — Model
- [x] Phase 7 — Training loop
- [x] Phase 8 — Sampling & eval
- [x] Phase 9 — SFT + demo

## Repo structure

```
marathi-gpt/
├── configs/            # nano / small / base model + training configs
├── data/               # download, clean, tokenizer training, pre-tokenization
├── model.py            # ~300-line decoder-only transformer
├── train.py            # single-file training loop
├── sample.py           # generation from checkpoints
├── eval/               # perplexity, few-shot sentiment, tokenizer fertility
├── sft/                # instruction-tuning data + fine-tuning
└── app/                # Gradio chat demo
```

## Setup

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate      # Windows
pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu128  # CUDA build; verified on RTX 5070
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## Quickstart

```bash
python data/download.py --source wikipedia --limit 1000   # drop --limit for the full source
python data/clean.py --limit 1000
python data/train_tokenizer.py --limit 1000 --vocab-size 1000  # drop both for a real 32k tokenizer
python data/prepare.py --limit 1000
python train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --benchmark     # pure throughput/MFU check, no data needed
python train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --max-steps 500 # a real (if small) training run
python sample.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt      # generate from prompts/gallery_mr.txt
python eval/perplexity.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt
python eval/mahasent_fewshot.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt --limit 300
python sft/build_instruct_data.py                           # pulls Marathi Dolly from ai4bharat/indic-align
python sft/finetune.py --checkpoint checkpoints/nano/best.pt --checkpoint-dir checkpoints/sft-nano
python app/gradio_demo.py --checkpoint checkpoints/sft-nano/best.pt
```

### First real training run

Ran the full pipeline end-to-end on the complete Marathi Wikipedia (94,133
articles) rather than a toy sample: `download.py --source wikipedia` (no
limit) → `clean.py` (54,895 docs survived langID/quality/dedup) →
`train_tokenizer.py --vocab-size 32000` (real 32k-vocab tokenizer, see
`assets/fertility_chart.png` — 4.8x fewer tokens than GPT-4's cl100k_base on
held-out Marathi) → `prepare.py` (33.1M train tokens after Wikipedia's 2x
upweight) → `train.py --config configs/nano.yaml --max-steps 500`.

Nano (22.9M params) trained in ~28 minutes on the RTX 5070: loss went
8.63 → 4.39 (train) / 4.59 (val) over 500 steps (262M tokens). Sample
generation at that checkpoint produces grammatical Marathi with correctly-
learned Wikipedia article structure (section headers like "इतिहास"/History,
"बाह्य दुवे"/External links) but falls into repetition loops on longer
continuations - expected for a 22.9M-param model this early in training, not
a bug.

Small (42.1M params) trained on the identical data/token budget (500 steps,
262M tokens) in ~89 minutes: loss went 8.69 → 4.25 (train) / 4.56 (val) -
modestly better than nano at the same budget, as expected for more params.
Its generations are noticeably more fluent: full, grammatically clean
sentences ("पुणे शहर हे येथील ऐतिहासिक शहर होते" - "Pune city was a historic
city here") and a correctly-reproduced Wikipedia city-article template
(इतिहास/History, भूगोल/Geography, हवामान/Climate, लोकसंख्या/Population
sections with plausible census-style demographic prose). One prompt still
degenerated into a nonsense numeral sequence - a real, honest failure mode at
this scale/budget, not cherry-picked away.

### Evaluation (Phase 8)

`eval/perplexity.py` walks the held-out splits exhaustively (non-overlapping
block_size chunks, not a sampled estimate) and reports perplexity separately
per split. On the small model:

| Split | Tokens | Loss | Perplexity |
|-------|--------|------|------------|
| val | 72,704 | 4.5596 | 95.55 |
| wiki_val | 388,096 | 4.6273 | 102.23 |

`eval/mahasent_fewshot.py` runs 3-shot sentiment classification on
[L3Cube MahaSent](https://github.com/l3cube-pune/MarathiNLP) (Marathi tweets,
3-class) by scoring label-word log-likelihoods - no fine-tuning, the model
just picks whichever label continuation it finds most probable. On 300 held-out
test tweets: **33.7% accuracy** (101/300) vs a 33.3% random baseline -
chance level. Expected and honest: the model has only ever seen Wikipedia
prose, never tweets or social-register text, and 42M params / 262M
pretraining tokens isn't enough to generalize zero-shot to an unseen domain
and label-verbalizer task. A real result, not swept under the rug.

### Instruction tuning & demo (Phase 9)

`sft/build_instruct_data.py` builds the SFT set from
[ai4bharat/indic-align](https://huggingface.co/datasets/ai4bharat/indic-align)'s
Marathi-translated Dolly split (IndicTrans2-translated by AI4Bharat) plus 18
hand-written examples in `sft/manual_examples.jsonl` (greetings, Marathi
proverbs, basic facts) - **14,950 train / 79 val** examples after holding out
examples longer than the model's context. (Anudesh, a second candidate
source, turned out to have an undocumented, non-parallel schema on inspection
- English-only `interactions` with no per-language columns - so it was left
out rather than risk silently training on English text; see the comment in
`build_instruct_data.py`.)

`sft/finetune.py` does a full fine-tune (42M params is small enough that
LoRA isn't necessary) of the small pretrained checkpoint, with the loss
masked to the assistant's response tokens only (not the `<|user|>` prompt).
2,796 steps (3 epochs, micro-batch 16, lr 2e-5 cosine) took **~8 minutes** on
the RTX 5070: val loss went 5.37 → **4.90**. Sample chat turns after SFT:

```
USER: नमस्कार, तू कोण आहेस?
ASSISTANT: मला मला सर्वात चांगले वाटते. मला वाटते की मला एक वाईट मत आहे...
  (grammatical Marathi, but repetitive and doesn't actually answer - typical
  small-model/small-SFT-budget failure mode)

USER: महाराष्ट्राची राजधानी कोणती आहे?
ASSISTANT: महाराष्ट्र
  (on-topic but incomplete/wrong - should be "मुंबई")

USER: एक छोटी मराठी कविता लिही.
ASSISTANT: सुरुवातीला, 'अ' हा सर्व कविता सादर करण्यासाठी, 'धाक्या' हा एक उत्तम
कथा दिग्दर्शन आणि दिग्दर्शन आहे.
  (fluent but not a coherent poem)
```

`app/gradio_demo.py` serves this checkpoint as a chat UI (smoke-tested: server
starts, serves the chat API, returns real generations end-to-end). Honest
summary: the model reliably speaks fluent, grammatical Marathi and follows
the chat format after SFT, but factual accuracy and coherence at this
scale (42M params, 262M pretraining tokens, ~15k SFT examples) are limited -
exactly what the plan's "portfolio scale, not production quality" framing
predicts, not a bug to fix.

## Model tiers

| Tier | Params (measured) | Layers / Heads / d_model | Context |
|------|--------------------|---------------------------|---------|
| nano  | 22.9M (53.6% tied embedding) | 6 / 6 / 384  | 512  |
| small | 42.1M (38.9% tied embedding) | 8 / 8 / 512  | 1024 |
| base  | 109.5M (22.4% tied embedding) | 12 / 12 / 768 | 1024 |

Original targets were ~15M/~50M/~124M; actual counts run a bit higher for the
smaller tiers because the 32,000-word tokenizer's tied embedding table
(vocab_size × n_embd) is a fixed cost that dominates a narrow model
disproportionately - it shrinks from 54% of nano's params to 22% of base's
as d_model grows. Not a bug, just an artifact of picking the vocab size
before the model width.

# Veritas
Status: complete
One-liner: A GraphRAG engine combining vector and graph retrieval, containerized with GPU passthrough and running fully local.

Stack: ChromaDB, Neo4j, Ollama, Gemma, Docker Compose
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Veritas

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Vector retrieval is good at "find me something similar" and bad at "how are these two things connected" — multi-hop questions where the answer lives in a relationship rather than in any single chunk. Veritas pairs ChromaDB for semantic recall with a Neo4j entity graph for relational traversal, so both query shapes have a path to an answer. The deployment side was the part that took real work: Docker Compose with GPU passthrough to keep Ollama inference on the local card while Neo4j and Chroma run alongside it, reproducibly, on one machine.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-07-28T20:23:21Z
- GitHub description: Privacy-first, self-hosted GraphRAG agent combining vector search (ChromaDB) with Neo4j knowledge-graph traversal for accurate, hallucination-resistant answers over technical documents — runs fully offline via Ollama and Docker.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 45337
- JavaScript: 20257
- CSS: 12061
- HTML: 7850
- Dockerfile: 1007

## README
# Veritas

A privacy-first, self-hosted **GraphRAG** engine. Documents are chunked and embedded into a
vector store *and* mined for entities/relationships into a knowledge graph, so every answer
can point to the exact subgraph it traversed to get there — not just a wall of retrieved text.

- **Vector search** — ChromaDB, embeddings via local Ollama (`nomic-embed-text`)
- **Knowledge graph** — Neo4j, entities/relationships extracted per chunk by a local LLM
- **Answer generation** — Ollama (Gemma 3) by default; optionally Gemini or Groq if you provide an API key
- **Web UI** — Flask + Jinja2 + vanilla JS (vis-network, marked.js) — no build step

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    U[Browser] -->|HTTP/SSE| FE[Flask webapp :8501]
    FE -->|proxy| API[FastAPI backend :8000]
    API --> CHROMA[(ChromaDB\nvector store)]
    API --> NEO4J[(Neo4j\nknowledge graph)]
    API --> OLLAMA[Ollama :11434\nGemma 3 / nomic-embed-text]
    API -.optional.-> GEMINI[Gemini API]
    API -.optional.-> GROQ[Groq API]
```

Question flow: the query is embedded and matched against Chroma; the chunks that come back are
used to seed a traversal into Neo4j (`Chunk -[:MENTIONS]-> Entity -[:RELATED_TO]-> Entity`); the
vector text + graph context are combined into a prompt and streamed back token-by-token, along
with the exact subgraph that was walked to build the answer.

## Ports

| Service | Container | Host port | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Web UI (Flask) | `frontend` | **8501** | main entrypoint |
| API (FastAPI) | `api` | **8000** | `/docs` for interactive Swagger UI |
| Neo4j Browser | `graph-db` | 7474 | `neo4j` / `veritas_password` |
| Neo4j Bolt | `graph-db` | 7687 | |
| Ollama | `llm-server` | 11434 | |
| ChromaDB (inspection only) | `vector-db` | 8001 | API talks to Chroma via a mounted local persist dir, not this port |

> The original Streamlit frontend called the API on port 8080 while the README documented 8000 —
> both the API and its Docker port mapping are now standardized on **8000**.

## Running it

### Docker Compose (recommended)

```bash
docker-compose up -d --build
```

Then open **http://localhost:8501**.

### Local dev (no Docker)

```bash
# terminal 1 - API (needs Neo4j + Ollama reachable at localhost)
cd backend
pip install -r requirements.txt
uvicorn main:app --reload --port 8000

# terminal 2 - web UI
cd webapp
pip install -r requirements.txt
export API_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8000   # Windows: set API_BASE_URL=...
flask --app app.py run --port 8501
```

## Choosing an LLM provider

Answer generation defaults to the **local Ollama** model — nothing about your question or
retrieved context leaves the machine unless you opt in to a hosted API. Document ingestion
(entity/relationship extraction) always uses local Ollama regardless of this setting.

| Env var | Default | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `LLM_PROVIDER` | `ollama` | `ollama` \| `gemini` \| `groq` |
| `OLLAMA_CHAT_MODEL` | `gemma3` | model served by the local Ollama container |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` | — | required to use `gemini` |
| `GEMINI_MODEL` | `gemini-2.5-flash` | |
| `GROQ_API_KEY` | — | required to use `groq` |
| `GROQ_MODEL` | `llama-3.1-70b-versatile` | |

Per-request overrides are also supported — pass `"provider": "gemini"` (and optionally `"model"`)
in the JSON body of `/ask`, `/ask/stream`, or `/ask/compare` to use a different provider for a
single question without changing the default.

## API reference

| Method & path | Description |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | Status of Neo4j, ChromaDB, Ollama, and the configured LLM providers |
| `POST /ask` | Non-streaming hybrid answer: `{query, provider?, model?, k?}` |
| `POST /ask/stream` | SSE token stream; final event carries sources, traversed subgraph, and timing |
| `POST /ask/compare` | Runs vector-only / graph-only / hybrid side by side |
| `GET /graph/overview?limit=200` | Sampled subgraph of the whole knowledge base, with counts |
| `GET /graph/node/{id}/neighbors` | Expand a node's neighbors (click-to-expand in the UI) |
| `POST /ingest/upload` | Upload a PDF/TXT/MD, runs the ingestion pipeline in the background |
| `GET /ingest/status/{job_id}` | Stage + running counts for an ingest job |
| `GET /documents` | List ingested documents with chunk/entity/relationship counts |
| `DELETE /documents/{name}` | Remove a document's chunks, vectors, and orphaned entities |

## Repo layout

```
backend/               FastAPI service
  main.py              API routes
  retrieval.py         shared vector + graph retrieval logic
  llm_providers.py     ollama / gemini / groq chat-model selection
  ingest.py            parsing -> chunking -> embedding -> entity extraction -> graph write
  test_api.py          endpoint smoke tests (mocked dependencies)
  test_agent.py        manual end-to-end script against a running API
webapp/                Flask UI (chat, ingest, graph explorer)
samples/               sample PDFs for trying out ingestion
docker-compose.yml
```

## Screenshots

_placeholder — add screenshots of the chat + graph panel, ingest progress, and explorer here._

---

Built by [Spandan Nagale](https://github.com/SpandanNagale).

# Self-Healing Hybrid RAG
Status: complete
One-liner: A hybrid retrieval pipeline that measures its own quality with RAGAS and repairs its index in the background when it degrades.

Stack: LangGraph, BM25, dense retrieval, RRF, cross-encoder reranking, RAGAS
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/self-healing-rag

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Retrieval quality decays after deployment — documents change, the corpus grows, embeddings go stale — and most RAG systems have no idea it's happening because nothing measures them after the demo. The retrieval stack itself is conventional and deliberate: dense plus BM25 fused with reciprocal rank fusion to cover both semantic and lexical matching, then a cross-encoder rerank on the fused candidates to buy precision at the top. The part worth talking about is the layer above it — RAGAS evaluation running against the live system, and a background job that heals the index when scores drop, instead of waiting for a user to complain.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-07-24T18:08:59Z
- GitHub description: A production-grade hybrid RAG system that detects its own retrieval failures and recovers automatically — combining vector search + page-level indexing with a self-correcting LangGraph pipeline that grades, retries, and verifies its own answers before responding

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 114026
- JavaScript: 16956
- CSS: 14419
- HTML: 6820

## README
# Self-Healing Hybrid RAG

A production-shaped Retrieval-Augmented Generation system built around two ideas:

1. **Hybrid retrieval** - every query fans out to a dense vector index (Qdrant) *and*
   a page/section-level keyword index (BM25) in parallel, fused with Reciprocal Rank
   Fusion and reranked with a cross-encoder.
2. **Self-healing** - a [LangGraph](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph) state
   machine grades its own retrieval quality and verifies its own answers against the
   retrieved context. When either check fails, it rewrites the query, widens context,
   or switches retrieval strategy - and only gives up with an explicit
   "insufficient context" if every recovery strategy is exhausted. It never silently
   hallucinates past a bad retrieval.

A separate background job mines the failure history this loop produces to find
documents that are *repeatedly* graded low-relevance, and automatically
re-chunks them with a different strategy - fixing bad ingestion decisions
without a human in the loop.

---

## Architecture

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Ingestion["Ingestion Pipeline"]
        direction TB
        U[Upload: PDF / DOCX / TXT / MD] --> P[Parse: pages, sections, tables]
        P --> H[Content hash per page/chunk]
        H --> C[Chunk: sliding window, configurable size/overlap]
        C --> V1[(Qdrant\nvector path)]
        P --> K1[(BM25\npage/section index)]
        H -. "unchanged hash -> skip re-embed" .-> V1
        H -. "unchanged hash -> skip re-tokenize" .-> K1
    end

    subgraph Query["Self-Healing Query Loop  (LangGraph)"]
        direction TB
        R[Retrieve\nhybrid: vector + keyword] --> RRF[RRF fusion + cross-encoder rerank]
        RRF --> G{Grade relevance}
        G -- relevant --> GEN[Generate\ngrounded answer + citations]
        G -- "low relevance\n(retries left)" --> RW[Rewrite / expand query]
        RW --> R
        G -- "retries exhausted" --> WS[Widen context /\nswitch vector<->keyword]
        WS --> G
        G -- "all strategies exhausted" --> INSUF[Return: insufficient context]
        GEN --> VER{Verify faithfulness}
        VER -- supported --> DONE[Return answer]
        VER -- "unsupported\n(retries left)" --> GEN2[Regenerate,\nstricter grounding]
        GEN2 --> VER
        VER -- "verify retries exhausted" --> RW
        INSUF --> DONE
    end

    Query -. "every low-relevance grade / failed verify" .-> FL[(Failure log\nJSONL)]

    subgraph Healing["Index Healing  (background job)"]
        direction TB
        FL --> AN[Analyze: count failures per doc_id]
        AN -- "doc exceeds\nfailure threshold" --> RC[Re-chunk + re-embed\nthat doc only, smaller chunk size]
        RC --> V1
        RC --> K1
    end

    V1 --> R
    K1 --> R
```

### Why this design

- **Two indexes, not one.** Dense vectors are great at paraphrase/semantic
  matches but blur exact numbers, table cells, and rare terms. A page-level
  BM25 index keeps those intact. RRF fusion means neither path has to be
  perfect alone.
- **The graph grades and verifies itself.** Most RAG demos assume retrieval
  worked and generation is grounded. This one checks both, explicitly, with
  the LLM acting as its own critic - and has a real recovery path (rewrite →
  widen/switch → give up honestly) instead of one shot at an answer.
- **Failure logs feed back into ingestion.** A single bad answer might just be
  a hard question. A document that shows up in low-relevance grades across
  many *different* queries is a chunking problem, not a question problem -
  that's the signal the index-healing job looks for.
- **Everything provider-specific is config, not code.** LLM and embedding
  providers are swapped via `.env` - see [Configuration](#configuration).

---

## Repo layout

```
app/
  config.py                 # pydantic-settings, env-driven
  dependencies.py           # wires every singleton together (Container)
  main.py                   # FastAPI app + lifespan (starts index-healing loop)
  models/schemas.py          # shared pydantic models (Chunk, RetrievedChunk, QueryResponse, ...)
  ingestion/
    parsers.py               # PDF (pdfplumber) / DOCX (python-docx) / text+markdown
    chunking.py              # sliding-window word chunker
    hashing.py                # content hashes -> incremental indexing
    registry.py                # per-doc metadata (storage path, chunk size used)
    pipeline.py                 # ties parse -> chunk -> diff -> index together
  embeddings/                 # local (sentence-transformers) | ollama | gemini
  llm/                         # ollama | ollama_cloud | gemini | groq
  retrieval/
    vector_store.py           # Qdrant wrapper (embedded-mode by default)
    keyword_store.py           # BM25 page-level index
    fusion.py                    # Reciprocal Rank Fusion
    reranker.py                   # cross-encoder reranking
    hybrid.py                      # ties it all together + widen/switch fallbacks
  graph/
    state.py, nodes.py, graph.py, prompts.py, runner.py   # the LangGraph state machine
  healing/
    failure_logger.py          # structured JSONL of every retry/failure
    index_healer.py              # analyzes failures, re-chunks bad docs
    scheduler.py                  # runs index_healer on an interval
  cache/semantic_cache.py     # embedding-similarity query cache
  observability/               # structured logging + RAGAS-style proxy metrics
  api/                           # FastAPI routers: /ingest, /query, /health, /metrics
tests/                           # pytest suite, incl. the self-healing demo scenario
scripts/run_demo.py             # narrated end-to-end demo against your real LLM
```

---

## Setup

### 1. Install dependencies

```bash
python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\activate        # Windows
# source .venv/bin/activate   # macOS/Linux

pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 2. Configure providers

```bash
cp .env.example .env
```

By default the system runs **entirely locally, no API keys required**:
- LLM: `ollama` (`qwen2.5:14b`) - install [Ollama](https://ollama.com), then:
  ```bash
  ollama pull qwen2.5:14b
  ollama serve
  ```
- Embeddings: `local` sentence-transformers (`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`), downloaded
  automatically on first run.
- Vector store: embedded/on-disk Qdrant (`./data/qdrant`) - no server needed.
- Keyword index: pure-Python BM25 (`rank_bm25`) - no server needed.

To use a hosted provider instead, edit `.env`:

| Setting | Options |
|---|---|
| `LLM_PROVIDER` | `ollama` (local) · `ollama_cloud` (hosted, needs `OLLAMA_CLOUD_API_KEY`) · `gemini` (needs `GEMINI_API_KEY`) · `groq` (needs `GROQ_API_KEY`) |
| `EMBEDDING_PROVIDER` | `local` (sentence-transformers) · `ollama` (local or cloud) · `gemini` |
| `QDRANT_URL` | leave empty for embedded mode, or point at a running Qdrant server |

Chunk sizes, retry limits, top-k, and cache thresholds are all in `.env` too -
see `.env.example` for the full list with comments.

### 3. Run the API + web UI

```bash
uvicorn app.main:app --reload
```

Then open **http://localhost:8000/** for the web UI (screenshots below), or
use the API directly:

- `POST /ingest` - multipart file upload (`file=@doc.pdf`), returns immediately
  with `{"doc_id", "status": "queued"}` while parsing/embedding happens in a
  background task.
- `GET /ingest/status/{doc_id}` - check whether a queued document has finished indexing.
- `GET /documents` / `DELETE /documents/{doc_id}` - list / remove ingested documents.
- `POST /query` - `{"query": "...", "doc_id": "optional-scope-to-one-doc"}`,
  returns the final `QueryResponse` in one shot.
- `POST /query/stream` - same pipeline, but pushed to the client node-by-node
  over Server-Sent Events as the graph actually executes (`data: {"type":
  "step", "node": "grade", "grade": "irrelevant", ...}` for each step, then a
  final `{"type": "final", ...}` with the full `QueryResponse`). This is what
  the web UI's live trace panel consumes - it is not a replay or animation,
  each event is emitted the moment that graph node finishes.
- `GET /config` / `POST /config` - read/update the active LLM and embedding
  provider+model at runtime (see [Web UI](#web-ui) below for the caveats around
  changing embeddings).
- `GET /config/ollama-models?cloud=false` - lists models actually available on
  the configured Ollama host, for the UI's model picker.
- `GET /health` - current provider config.
- `GET /metrics` - query counts, cache hit rate, faithfulness/relevance proxy
  metrics, retrieval-strategy usage.

## Web UI

A single-page UI (`static/index.html` + `style.css` + `app.js`, no build
step, no framework - served directly by FastAPI's `StaticFiles`) is designed
so someone with no RAG background can watch the self-healing loop happen and
understand *why* each step occurred, not just see a final answer:

- **Documents panel** - drag-and-drop upload, live indexed/queued status,
  per-document page/chunk counts, remove button.
- **Ask panel** - a question box and an optional "scope to one document" picker.
- **"How it's thinking" panel** - the real live trace from `/query/stream`,
  translated into plain language per step ("Rewriting the question (attempt
  1)... retrieval wasn't good enough, so the query is being reformulated to:
  ...", "Double-checking the answer... ✅ Fully supported by the retrieved
  passages."), color-coded by outcome (relevant/verified = green, retry in
  progress = amber, gave up = red).
- **Answer panel** - the grounded answer, citation chips (doc + page +
  section), and the retry count / strategy used / verification result for
  that specific answer.
- **System health panel** - live `/metrics` snapshot (query count, cache hit
  rate, faithfulness proxy, average retries).
- **Provider settings drawer** - switch LLM provider (Ollama local / Ollama
  Cloud / Gemini / Groq) and model at runtime, with an Ollama model picker
  populated from whatever's actually pulled on the configured host. Embedding
  provider/model can also be changed here, but since a different embedding
  model means an incompatible vector space, doing so **clears the vector
  index, keyword index, and document registry** and requires re-ingesting -
  the UI shows this warning before/after applying the change.

Visual style is a "liquid glass" look: translucent, blurred glass panels
(`backdrop-filter: blur() saturate()`) over an animated dark gradient
background, consistent across every panel and the settings drawer.

| Initial state | Answer + live trace | Provider settings |
|---|---|---|
| ![Initial state](docs/screenshots/01_initial.png) | ![Answer and trace](docs/screenshots/02_answer.png) | ![Provider settings drawer](docs/screenshots/03_settings.png) |

### 4. Run the tests

```bash
pytest
```

The test suite uses fake (offline, deterministic) embedding and LLM providers
so it runs without Ollama, API keys, or model downloads - see `tests/fakes.py`.

---

## The self-healing loop, demonstrated

### Guaranteed-deterministic version (CI)

```bash
pytest tests/test_self_healing_demo.py -v
```

`test_self_healing_recovers_after_failed_first_retrieval` ingests a short
policy document and asks a question phrased with vocabulary that shares no
terms with the source text ("money back timeframe" vs. a document that talks
about "refunds... processed... business days"). Walking through what actually
happens:

1. **Retrieve** (hybrid, original query) - BM25 finds zero token overlap; the
   embedding path returns only weak matches.
2. **Grade** - flagged `irrelevant`. Logged to the failure log.
3. **Rewrite** - query becomes `"refund business days processing time"`.
4. **Retrieve** (hybrid, rewritten query) - now BM25 and vector search both
   land on the *Refund Policy* section.
5. **Grade** - `relevant`.
6. **Generate** - grounded answer with an inline citation.
7. **Verify** - answer checked against the retrieved passage, passes.

Final response: `retries=1`, `insufficient_context=False`, answer contains
the correct figure, citation points at the right page. A second test in the
same file (`test_query_that_never_recovers_returns_insufficient_context`)
proves the other half of the contract: when nothing in the corpus is
relevant, the system returns an explicit "insufficient context" message
instead of guessing.

### Real end-to-end version (your configured LLM)

```bash
python scripts/run_demo.py
```

Runs the same shape of scenario against whatever LLM/embedding provider is in
your `.env` (local Ollama by default), against a small travel-expense policy
doc with a deliberate decoy section, and prints the full node-by-node trace.
Because it's a real model instead of a scripted one, the exact retry count can
vary run to run - that's expected and is why the pytest version above is the
reproducible source of truth.

### Index healing

`tests/test_index_healing.py` shows the other half of the self-healing story:
after a document accumulates enough low-relevance grades across different
queries (`INDEX_HEALING_FAILURE_THRESHOLD`, default 3), the background job
(`app/healing/index_healer.py`) re-chunks and re-embeds *that document only*
with a smaller chunk size - without touching any other document in the index,
and without a query ever asking for it directly.

---

## Configuration reference

See `.env.example` for the complete, commented list. Key knobs:

| Variable | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `CHUNK_SIZE` / `CHUNK_OVERLAP` | Word-count sliding window for the vector path |
| `RETRIEVAL_TOP_K` / `RERANK_TOP_K` | Candidates fused per path / kept after reranking |
| `MAX_REWRITE_RETRIES` | How many times the graph rewrites+re-retrieves before falling back to widen/switch |
| `MAX_VERIFY_RETRIES` | How many times generation is retried with stricter grounding before falling back to a retrieval retry |
| `GRADE_RELEVANCE_THRESHOLD` | Reserved for a future numeric grader; current grader is categorical (relevant/partial/irrelevant) |
| `INDEX_HEALING_INTERVAL_SECONDS` | How often the background healing job runs |
| `INDEX_HEALING_FAILURE_THRESHOLD` | Low-relevance grades (across distinct queries) before a doc gets re-chunked |
| `SEMANTIC_CACHE_THRESHOLD` | Cosine similarity above which a query is treated as a cache hit |

## Known limitations

- BM25 index rebuilds its ranking structure on every write (cheap - it skips
  re-tokenizing unchanged pages, but there's no true incremental posting-list
  update like a real search engine would have).
- Embedded Qdrant (file-backed, no server) is single-process; point
  `QDRANT_URL` at a real Qdrant deployment for multi-worker/production use.
- Metrics are proxies computed from the graph's own grade/verify calls, not
  full RAGAS (which would require its own separate LLM-judge calls per query).
- Ingestion runs as an in-process `BackgroundTasks` job, not a durable queue -
  a process restart mid-ingestion loses that job (acceptable for this scope;
  swap in Celery+Redis if you need durability across restarts).

# CrewAI Research Pipeline Status: complete One-liner: A four-agent research system — Planner, Researcher, Writer, Critic — with LLM-as-Judge scoring and streamed intermediate output. Stack: CrewAI, ChromaDB, SSE, Python Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/crewai-research-pipeline ## Design rationale (why it was built this way) Splitting research into Planner, Researcher, Writer, and Critic roles keeps each agent's context narrow enough to stay reliable, and makes the failure visible when it happens — you can see which stage produced the bad output instead of debugging one long opaque generation. The Critic runs an LLM-as-Judge pass over the draft rather than the pipeline simply terminating on the Writer's first output, and SSE streaming exposes every intermediate stage to the user, which turns a black box into something inspectable. This was later extended into an Enterprise AI Research Agent for a take-home assignment. ## Anticipated questions Q: Isn't LLM-as-Judge just the same model grading itself? A: Largely, yes — that's the known weakness, and it's why the Critic here scores drafts rather than gating anything destructive. DataSleuth uses execution-based verification precisely because judgment-based verification wasn't strong enough for that use case. ## Repository facts (from GitHub) - Stars: 0 - Last commit: 2026-08-13T13:26:26Z - GitHub description: Production-ready multi-agent research API built with CrewAI + Gemma 4. Features a FastAPI backend, Server-Sent Events (SSE) streaming, and an automated eval scorer for citation, coverage, and clarity. ## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub) - Python: 78619 - CSS: 9890 - JavaScript: 7139 - HTML: 6044 ## README # NeuroSearch: Enterprise Multi-Agent Research & Evaluation Pipeline NeuroSearch is an autonomous, multi-agent research pipeline powered by **CrewAI** and pluggable Large Language Models (local **Gemma** via **Ollama** by default, with optional **Ollama Cloud** and **Groq** backends). A team of specialized AI agents plans, researches, cross-checks, classifies, and writes comprehensive, well-cited reports on any topic — and every finding, source, contradiction, and conclusion is persisted to a structured SQLite database so the whole reasoning chain stays traceable and reusable. This project features three distinct interfaces: 1. 🖥️ **Live surveillance Web UI** (Flask-based dashboard with real-time agent output streaming via Server-Sent Events) 2. ⚡ **Headless REST API** (FastAPI backend with streaming, traceability, and knowledge-search endpoints) 3. ⌨️ **Command-Line Interface** (CLI script for terminal operation) --- ## 🏗️ Architecture & Workflow Before running full research, an incoming topic is embedded and compared against past `research_questions` in ChromaDB (knowledge reuse). If nothing close enough exists, the pipeline runs end-to-end, writing every stage's output to the database as it goes — not just at the end: ```mermaid graph TD User([User Topic]) --> Reuse{Similar question
already answered?} Reuse -->|Yes, above threshold| Existing[Return existing findings
+ conclusions from DB] Reuse -->|No| Planner[Research Planner] Planner -->|Sub-questions| Researcher[Research Analyst] Researcher -->|Atomic findings, one per source
written to sources + findings tables| Comparator[Evidence Comparator] Comparator -->|Contradictions written to
contradictions table| Classifier[Findings Classifier] Classifier -->|Category written to
findings.category| Writer[Technical Writer] Writer -->|Reads findings/contradictions
from DB, mentions them explicitly| Report[Markdown Report + Conclusion] Report --> Output[Save to file + conclusions table] Output --> Scorer[LLM Judge / Scorer
separate final-stage eval] Scorer -->|Citation, Coverage, Clarity| User ``` ### 👥 The Research Team | Agent | Role | Focus / Goal | Tools Used | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Research Planner** | `Research Planner` | Decompose topic into 4–6 specific, focused sub-questions. | None (analytical reasoning) | | **Research Analyst** | `Research Analyst` | Extract atomic, single-claim findings — each tied to exactly one source — for every sub-question. | Web Search (Serper or DuckDuckGo), Wikipedia | | **Evidence Comparator** | `Evidence Comparator` | Cross-check findings answering the same sub-question, flag genuine disagreements. | None (reads findings from DB) | | **Findings Classifier** | `Findings Classifier` | Tag every finding with a category (adoption, technology, risk, regulatory, case-study, other). | None (reads findings from DB) | | **Technical Writer** | `Technical Writer` | Synthesize *only* from findings/conclusions in the DB; explicitly calls out contradictions rather than silently resolving them. | None (reads findings/contradictions from DB) | > The original single **Quality Critic** step has been split into the Evidence Comparator and Classifier above, which now run *before* the Writer instead of editing the report *after* it. `agents/critic.py` / `tasks/critique_task.py` remain in the codebase but are no longer part of the default pipeline. The LLM-as-judge evaluation in `eval/scorer.py` (citation/coverage/clarity) is a separate, final-stage quality check — it does not merge with the two stages above. --- ## 📁 Project Structure ``` research-pipeline/ ├── agents/ # Agent definition scripts │ ├── base.py # Thin wrapper around llm/provider.py's get_llm() │ ├── planner.py # Research Planner agent │ ├── researcher.py # Research Analyst agent (with web/wiki tools) │ ├── evidence_comparator.py # Evidence Comparator agent (contradiction detection) │ ├── classifier.py # Findings Classifier agent │ ├── writer.py # Technical Writer agent │ └── critic.py # Legacy — kept, no longer wired into the pipeline ├── tasks/ # Tasks assigned to agents │ ├── schemas.py # Pydantic output schemas (structured LLM outputs) │ ├── plan_task.py # Formulating research objectives │ ├── research_task.py # Extracting atomic findings + citations │ ├── compare_task.py # Cross-checking findings for contradictions │ ├── classify_task.py # Tagging findings by category │ ├── write_task.py # Writing the markdown report from DB findings │ └── critique_task.py # Legacy — kept, no longer wired into the pipeline ├── db/ # Structured persistence / traceability layer │ ├── models.py # SQLAlchemy models (see schema below) │ ├── session.py # Engine/session factory, init_db() │ └── repository.py # All reads/writes — returns plain dicts ├── llm/ # LLM provider abstraction │ └── provider.py # LLMProvider interface + get_llm() factory ├── tools/ # Tools utilized by agents │ ├── search_tool.py # SearchProvider-backed CrewAI tool, with fallback │ ├── providers/ # SearchProvider interface + implementations │ │ ├── base.py # SearchProvider ABC │ │ ├── serper_provider.py # Google results via Serper.dev (needs a key) │ │ └── duckduckgo_provider.py # Free, no-key fallback │ ├── wiki_tool.py # Wikipedia search wrapper │ └── file_tool.py # Helper to write reports to disk ├── memory/ # ChromaDB-backed vector memory │ ├── vector_store.py # Generic persistent embedding collection │ └── reuse.py # Knowledge reuse check + /knowledge/search index ├── worker/ # Async job scaffolding │ └── job_manager.py # In-process ThreadPoolExecutor job runner ├── eval/ # LLM-as-a-judge evaluation suite (final-stage, separate) │ └── scorer.py # Automated scoring for citation, coverage, clarity ├── config/ # Settings and parameters │ ├── settings.py # App settings & dotenv loader │ └── agents_config.yaml # Agent roles/goals/backstories + per-agent LLM overrides ├── templates/ / static/ # Flask Web UI assets ├── outputs/ # Finished research reports (markdown) ├── research.db # SQLite traceability DB (gitignored, created on first run) ├── chroma_db/ # ChromaDB vector store (gitignored) ├── app.py # FastAPI REST API ├── flask_app.py # Flask Web UI server ├── main.py # Command-line interface ├── requirements.txt # Dependency declarations ├── .env.example # Documented template for all environment variables └── .env # Local environment settings (gitignored) ``` --- ## ⚙️ Setup & Installation ### 1. Prerequisites - **Python 3.10** or higher. - **Ollama** installed and running locally — this is the zero-cost default; no cloud API key is required to run NeuroSearch end-to-end. ### 2. Configure Local LLM ```bash ollama pull gemma3:12b ``` ### 3. Clone & Install Dependencies ```bash python -m venv venv # Windows: .\venv\Scripts\activate # Linux/macOS: source venv/bin/activate pip install -r requirements.txt ``` ### 4. Configure Environment Variables Copy the template and edit as needed: ```bash cp .env.example .env ``` The defaults run everything locally with **no API keys**. See [LLM Providers](#-llm-providers) and [Search Provider & Fallback](#-search-provider--fallback) below for the opt-in cloud options. --- ## 🚀 How to Run ### A. Terminal Interface (CLI) ```bash python main.py "The impact of AI on drug discovery in 2024" --eval ``` - `--eval` scores the final report after generation. - `--force` skips the knowledge-reuse check and always runs fresh research, even if a near-duplicate question already exists in the DB. ### B. Interactive Web UI (Flask) ```bash python flask_app.py ``` Open **`http://127.0.0.1:5000`**, type a topic, and watch the live agent trace stream in. ### C. FastAPI Backend REST API ```bash uvicorn app:app --reload --port 8000 ``` Interactive docs at **`http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs`**. | Endpoint | Description | | :--- | :--- | | `POST /research` | Run the full pipeline, writing every stage to the DB. Returns the report plus `question_id`, `reused`, `findings_count`, `contradictions_count`. | | `POST /research/stream` | Same pipeline, streamed as SSE. | | `POST /research/async` | Returns `{job_id}` immediately; pipeline runs in a background thread. | | `GET /jobs/{job_id}` | Poll status/result of an async job (`pending` / `running` / `done` / `failed`). | | `GET /questions/{id}/trace` | Full traceability chain: conclusion(s) → the findings each was derived from → their sources. | | `GET /questions/{id}/contradictions` | All contradictions flagged for a question. | | `GET /knowledge/search?q=` | Semantic search over every past finding/conclusion. | | `POST /eval` | Score an existing report without re-running the pipeline. | All request bodies accept `{"topic": "...", "evaluate": false, "force_rerun": false}`. --- ## 🗄️ Traceability & Persistence Layer Every research run is stored in a SQLite database (`db/models.py`, default `research.db`) with five tables that form a complete evidence chain: ``` research_questions (id, topic, sub_questions[json], created_at) │ ├─▶ sources (id, question_id, url, title, retrieved_at, raw_content) │ │ │ └─▶ findings (id, source_id, question_id, sub_question, text, category, created_at) │ │ │ ├─▶ contradictions (id, finding_a_id, finding_b_id, explanation) │ │ │ └─▶ conclusions (id, question_id, text, finding_ids[json], created_at) ``` - Every **finding** stores the `source_id` it came from — you can always answer "where did this claim come from?" - Every **conclusion** stores the `finding_ids` it was derived from — you can always answer "what evidence backs this conclusion?" - **Contradictions** link two findings with an explanation, so disagreements between sources are recorded rather than silently dropped. Query the chain via the API: ```bash curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/questions/1/trace curl http://127.0.0.1:8000/questions/1/contradictions curl "http://127.0.0.1:8000/knowledge/search?q=AI%20drug%20discovery%20risk" ``` ### Knowledge reuse Before running full research, the topic is embedded and compared (cosine similarity, ChromaDB) against every past `research_questions.topic`. If the best match is at or above `KNOWLEDGE_REUSE_THRESHOLD` (default `0.87`, configurable in `.env`), the existing findings/conclusions/contradictions are returned instead of re-running the pipeline — `reused: true` in the response. Pass `force_rerun: true` (API) or `--force` (CLI) to bypass this and always research fresh. --- ## 🔌 LLM Providers Every agent gets its LLM from a single factory (`llm/provider.py`), selected via `LLM_PROVIDER` in `.env`. **Local Ollama is the default and requires no API key.** Cloud providers are strictly opt-in. | `LLM_PROVIDER` | Cost | Where to get a key | Notes | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `ollama_local` (default) | Free | — | Runs entirely on your machine via `OLLAMA_BASE_URL` (default `localhost:11434`). No rate limits beyond your hardware. | | `ollama_cloud` | Free/paid tiers | `ollama signin` at [ollama.com](https://ollama.com) | Same Ollama API, hosted — set `OLLAMA_API_KEY`. Useful when local hardware can't run the model. | | `groq` | Free tier, then paid | [console.groq.com/keys](https://console.groq.com/keys) | Fast hosted inference (e.g. `llama-3.3-70b-versatile`). Free tier has request-per-minute limits — see Groq's console for current limits. | Per-agent overrides live in `config/agents_config.yaml` (e.g. a fast Groq model for the Planner/Classifier, a larger model for the Writer): ```yaml planner: llm_provider: groq llm_model: llama-3.1-8b-instant ``` Any agent without an override falls back to the global `LLM_PROVIDER` / `LLM_MODEL` in `.env`. **If a provider becomes unavailable** (auth error, timeout, rate limit), the pipeline does **not** silently return an empty report: the failing stage raises a `PipelineStageError` naming the stage and the underlying error, the API returns `502` with that detail, and the CLI/Flask paths surface the same message. There is no automatic cross-provider fallback for the LLM (unlike search, below) — switch `LLM_PROVIDER` in `.env` or fix the credentials and re-run. --- ## 🔍 Search Provider & Fallback The Research Analyst's web search is abstracted behind a `SearchProvider` interface (`tools/providers/`), selected via `SEARCH_PROVIDER`: - `serper` — Google results via [serper.dev](https://serper.dev) (free tier, requires `SERPER_API_KEY`). - `duckduckgo` — free, no API key, via the `ddgs` package. - `auto` (default) — uses Serper if `SERPER_API_KEY` is set, otherwise DuckDuckGo. This keeps a fresh clone fully runnable with zero keys. If the configured provider's request fails at runtime (network error, rate limit, bad key), `tools/search_tool.py` logs the failure and automatically retries the query against DuckDuckGo before giving up — so a transient Serper outage degrades search quality rather than failing the whole pipeline. --- ## 📈 Scaling from ~10 to 100,000 Questions The current setup (`worker/job_manager.py` + SQLite) is deliberately minimal so the project stays free and locally runnable. To scale: 1. **Queue-based workers.** `POST /research/async` already returns a `job_id` and runs the pipeline off the request thread via a `ThreadPoolExecutor`. Swap `job_manager.submit()` for a Celery `task.delay()` call backed by Redis or RabbitMQ, and run `celery -A worker worker` processes that can scale horizontally. Job status would move from the in-memory dict to a Redis hash or a `jobs` DB table so it survives restarts and is visible across processes. 2. **Postgres migration.** `DATABASE_URL` is the only thing that needs to change (`db/session.py` reads it directly) — point it at `postgresql+psycopg2://...` for concurrent writers, connection pooling, and indexing at volume. The SQLAlchemy models are dialect-agnostic. 3. **Caching via knowledge reuse.** The ChromaDB similarity check in `memory/reuse.py` already acts as a cache — as the corpus of past questions grows, an increasing fraction of new questions can be answered from `research_questions`/`findings`/`conclusions` without invoking any LLM or search call at all. At high volume this is the single biggest cost lever. 4. **Read scaling.** The `/questions/{id}/trace`, `/contradictions`, and `/knowledge/search` endpoints are pure reads — put them behind a cache (Redis) or read replica once `research_questions` grows past what a single Postgres instance comfortably serves. --- ## 📊 Evaluation Metrics After generating a report, the scoring module (`eval/scorer.py`) uses an isolated judge model instance (its own optional `evaluator` override in `agents_config.yaml`) to grade the report on three indices: 1. **Citation Score (40% Weight)**: Verifies if claims are backed by source references and links. 2. **Coverage Score (35% Weight)**: Evaluates depth, breadth, and how comprehensively sub-questions were answered. 3. **Clarity Score (25% Weight)**: Examines spelling, layout structure, logic, and readability. The scores are aggregated into a weighted average total score out of 10.0, along with direct feedback from the judge model. This step is intentionally separate from the Evidence Comparator/Classifier stages — it grades the finished report, not the intermediate findings. --- ## 🛠️ Customization To adjust agent personalities, goals, or LLM backends: 1. Open [`config/agents_config.yaml`](./config/agents_config.yaml). 2. Modify the `role`, `goal`, or `backstory` parameters, or add `llm_provider` / `llm_model` / `llm_temperature` to override that agent's LLM. 3. Restart your server/script.

# JARVIS
Status: complete
One-liner: A fully local voice assistant — wake word, speech recognition, LLM, tools, memory, screen vision, and speech synthesis — with nothing leaving the machine.

Stack: openWakeWord, faster-whisper large-v3-turbo, Qwen3:14b, Ollama, Piper TTS, ChromaDB, qwen2.5vl:7b
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/JARVIS

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Every commercial voice assistant streams your microphone to someone else's servers. This one doesn't: openWakeWord listens for "hey jarvis" locally, faster-whisper large-v3-turbo transcribes, Qwen3:14b reasons, Piper synthesizes speech, and ChromaDB holds conversational memory — all on one consumer GPU. The engineering constraint is latency budget. A voice loop feels broken past roughly two seconds, and there are five sequential stages competing for that window, so model selection at each stage was a latency-versus-quality decision rather than a pick-the-best-model decision. It also has tool access (DuckDuckGo, GitHub, Wikipedia) and screen vision via qwen2.5vl:7b, so it can answer questions about what's currently on the display.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-07-22T19:22:41Z
- GitHub description: Local voice assistant with wake word, GPU STT, Ollama tool-calling, PC control, memory, and web search — built for Windows.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 80366

## README
# ARIA — Local AI Voice Assistant

> A fully offline, voice-activated AI assistant for Windows, powered by **Ollama** (Qwen3:14b), **faster-whisper** (speech-to-text), **Coqui XTTS-v2** (text-to-speech, with Piper as a fallback), and **openWakeWord** (wake word detection) — with a live HUD overlay.

---

## ✨ Features

| Category | Capability |
|---|---|
| 🎙️ **Voice** | "Hey Aria" wake word · hold-Space push-to-talk · XTTS-v2 natural voice (voice cloning supported) with Piper fallback |
| 🖥️ **HUD** | Always-on-top overlay — idle / listening / thinking / speaking states, live transcript + reply text |
| 🧠 **AI** | Qwen3:14b via Ollama · adaptive chain-of-thought (`/think` / `/no_think`) |
| 🖥️ **System Control** | Open/close apps · volume · brightness · lock PC · list windows |
| 🌐 **Network** | DuckDuckGo web search · fetch web pages · GitHub search · Wikipedia |
| 👁️ **Vision** | Screenshot analysis, on-screen text reading (qwen2.5vl:7b) |
| 💾 **Memory** | ChromaDB-backed persistent facts · cross-session conversation history |
| 🛠️ **Coding** | Fuzzy file finder · code reader · explain code · refactor suggestions · traceback diagnosis |

> **Note on the wake word:** `hey_aria.onnx` is a custom openWakeWord model trained
> (via [openWakeWord's training pipeline](https://github.com/dscripka/openWakeWord))
> on synthetic TTS speech + real-world negative audio in a separate Linux/WSL environment
> (not part of this repo). It's a fast first-pass model rather than a heavily-tuned one —
> `WAKE_THRESHOLD` in `aria.py` is set conservatively (`0.6`) to keep false triggers down,
> at some cost to recall. If it feels sluggish to trigger, lower the threshold; if it fires
> on unrelated speech, raise it. Retraining with a larger synthetic dataset (more samples
> per phrase, more negative audio) would improve both.

---

## 🏗️ Project Structure

```
ARIA/
├── aria.py                    # Main entry point — run this
├── config.py                  # Shared constants (Ollama model name)
├── tools/                     # LLM-callable tool modules
│   ├── coding.py               # Find file, explain, refactor, diagnose traceback
│   ├── memory.py               # ChromaDB memory layer + session persistence
│   ├── network.py              # Web search, fetch page, GitHub, Wikipedia
│   └── vision.py               # Screenshot analysis via a vision model
├── voice/
│   └── tts.py                  # XTTS-v2 voice output, layered GPU/CPU/Piper fallback
├── ui/
│   └── hud.py                  # Always-on-top HUD overlay (PySide6)
├── hey_aria.onnx               # Custom-trained wake word model + hey_aria.onnx.data
├── wake_debug.py              # Utility to debug wake word detection scores
├── requirements.txt           # Python dependencies
└── memory/                    # ChromaDB storage (auto-created, gitignored)
```

> **`aria.py` is the only file you run.**

---

## ⚙️ Requirements

### Hardware
- **GPU**: NVIDIA GPU with CUDA support — recommended for faster-whisper `large-v3-turbo` and XTTS-v2. This project is tuned for a 12GB-class card (RTX 5070); XTTS's GPU fallback chain (see `voice/tts.py`) exists because VRAM gets tight once Ollama's model is also resident.
- **RAM**: 16 GB+ recommended (Qwen3:14b needs ~10 GB VRAM)
- **Microphone**: Any standard microphone

### Software
- Python 3.12
- [Ollama](https://ollama.com/) installed and running
- [Piper TTS](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper) binary on your `PATH` (fallback voice)
- CUDA Toolkit (for GPU-accelerated STT/TTS)

---

## 🚀 Setup

### 1. Clone the repository

```bash
git clone https://github.com/SpandanNagale/ARIA.git
cd ARIA
```

### 2. Create and activate a virtual environment

```bash
python -m venv venv

# Windows
venv\Scripts\activate

# macOS / Linux
source venv/bin/activate
```

### 3. Install dependencies

```bash
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

> **RTX 50-series (Blackwell) GPUs:** `requirements.txt` already pins `torch==2.9.1+cu128` and
> pulls from the PyTorch cu128 wheel index — needed for Blackwell (`sm_120`) support. It also
> pins `transformers<5` (a newer `transformers` breaks XTTS-v2's loader) and adds `torchcodec`
> (required by `torchaudio>=2.9`'s audio backend). If you hit GPU/DLL issues on a different card
> or driver, these are the first pins to double-check.

### 4. Pull the Ollama models

```bash
ollama pull qwen3:14b
ollama pull qwen2.5vl:7b   # optional, for screen/vision tools
```

### 5. XTTS-v2 voice setup

XTTS-v2's weights (~1.8GB) download automatically on first run — no manual step needed. Two options:

- **Default voice** (no setup): just run the project, XTTS uses a built-in speaker.
- **Voice cloning**: record a 6–10 second, single-speaker, quiet-room WAV sample, save it as
  `reference.wav` in the project root. `voice/tts.py` will use it automatically if present.

Piper remains as the automatic fallback if XTTS fails to load or errors mid-session — download
the `en_US-sam-medium` voice and place both files in the project root:

```
en_US-sam-medium.onnx
en_US-sam-medium.onnx.json
```

Download from: https://github.com/rhasspy/piper/releases

### 6. (Optional) Set a GitHub token for higher API rate limits

```bash
# Windows PowerShell
$env:GITHUB_TOKEN = "your_token_here"

# Linux / macOS
export GITHUB_TOKEN="your_token_here"
```

---

## ▶️ Running ARIA

```bash
python aria.py
```

ARIA will load the wake word model, STT model, and XTTS-v2, then open the HUD overlay and start listening.

**Activation modes:**
- Say **"Hey Aria"** → auto-detects and starts recording your command
- Hold **Spacebar** → push-to-talk mode

**HUD controls:**
- **Ctrl+Alt+H** → toggle the overlay on/off
- **Left-click + drag** → reposition
- **Mouse wheel** (while hovering it) → resize

Press `Ctrl+C` to quit.

---

## 🗣️ Example Commands

```
"Hey Aria, what time is it?"
"Hey Aria, open notepad."
"Hey Aria, set volume to 50."
"Hey Aria, set brightness to 80."
"Hey Aria, lock the PC."
"Hey Aria, search for Python async tutorials."
"Hey Aria, what is RAG in AI?"
"Hey Aria, search me on GitHub."
"Hey Aria, find repos for LangChain."
"Hey Aria, explain my aria.py file."
"Hey Aria, remember that I prefer dark mode."
"Hey Aria, what do you know about me?"
"Hey Aria, what's on my screen?"
```

---

## 🧩 Architecture

```
User Voice
    │
    ▼
openWakeWord ──► wake detected?
    │                  │
    │           faster-whisper (STT)
    │                  │
    │           User text ──────────────► ui.hud (live transcript)
    │                  │
    │           should_think()?
    │            /think or /no_think
    │                  │
    │           Ollama (Qwen3:14b)
    │                  │
    │           Tool calls?──► Tool implementations
    │                  │          (system / coding / memory / network / vision)
    │           Final reply ────────────► ui.hud (live reply + state)
    │                  │
    ▼         XTTS-v2 (GPU→CPU→Piper fallback) ──► Audio playback
ChromaDB ◄──── save_messages()
(memory)
```

The voice loop (`aria.py`'s `chat_loop`) runs on a background thread; the HUD's Qt event loop
owns the main thread. State updates flow one-way through a thread-safe queue (`ui.hud.push(...)`).

---

## 📦 Key Dependencies

| Package | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ollama` | Local LLM inference via Ollama |
| `faster-whisper` | GPU-accelerated speech-to-text |
| `openwakeword` | "Hey Aria" wake word detection |
| `coqui-tts` | XTTS-v2 text-to-speech (natural voice, cloning support) |
| `piper-tts` | Offline text-to-speech (fallback voice) |
| `torch` / `torchaudio` / `torchcodec` | GPU inference backend for XTTS-v2 |
| `PySide6` | HUD overlay (Qt) |
| `sounddevice` / `soundfile` | Audio I/O |
| `chromadb` | Persistent vector memory |
| `duckduckgo-search` | Web search (no API key needed) |
| `beautifulsoup4` | Web page text extraction |
| `requests` | HTTP (GitHub, Wikipedia, fetch) |
| `Pillow` | Screenshot capture for vision tools |
| `pycaw` | Windows audio volume control |
| `screen_brightness_control` | Monitor brightness control |
| `pygetwindow` | List open windows |
| `pyperclip` | Clipboard access for coding tools |
| `keyboard` | Spacebar push-to-talk + HUD toggle hotkey |

---

## 📁 What's Gitignored

| Item | Reason |
|---|---|
| `venv/` | Virtual environment (recreate with `pip install -r requirements.txt`) |
| `*.onnx` / `*.onnx.json` | Piper voice model (~60 MB) — download separately |
| `*.wav` | Runtime audio files generated by TTS, and any `reference.wav` voice sample |
| `memory/` | ChromaDB data — user-specific, created at runtime |
| `.env` | Secrets (e.g. `GITHUB_TOKEN`) |

---

## 🤝 Contributing

Pull requests are welcome! For major changes, please open an issue first to discuss what you'd like to change.

---

One-liner: A deployed tool that measures how context window size affects answer quality when querying a codebase.

Stack: Next.js 15, TypeScript, Groq, GitHub API
Live URL: https://context-lense.vercel.app
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Context_lense

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
"More context is better" is assumed more often than it's measured. ContextLens tests it directly on codebases — varying how much of a repo goes into the window and measuring what happens to answer quality, which surfaces the point where additional context stops helping and starts diluting. Built as a take-home assignment for Open Gigantic, and the one project in the portfolio that's a deployed TypeScript/Next.js app rather than a local Python system.

## README
# ContextLens

ContextLens measures the tradeoff between **context size** and **answer quality** when asking questions about a codebase.

You paste a public GitHub repo URL (or pick a pre-indexed demo) and ask one question about the code. ContextLens answers it **twice** using two different context strategies and shows both side by side:

- **Naive path** — score *files* by keyword/path relevance, dump their full contents into the prompt.
- **Compressed path** — build a *symbol-level* map, select only the relevant symbols plus their direct dependencies, summarize the rest, and send a much smaller prompt.

For each path you see the **token count sent, estimated cost, latency, and the model's answer**, plus a collapsible panel showing exactly what context was sent. A prominent delta readout shows how many fewer tokens/cost the compressed path used.

> **The point is the measurement, not the compression.** A result showing compression degrades quality on certain question types is a *success*, not a failure. See [The honest eval](#the-honest-eval).

## Stack

- Next.js 15 (App Router) + TypeScript + Tailwind v4
- LLM via **Anthropic** or **Groq** — server-side only, key in env var, never exposed to the client
- **GitHub REST API** for ingestion (no `git clone` — serverless has no persistent disk)
- **js-tiktoken** (`cl100k_base`) for accurate token counts
- **SSE** for streaming progress and answers

## Demo (zero setup)

Two demo repos are **pre-indexed as static JSON** in `src/data/` and committed to the repo. A reviewer can click a demo chip, pick a suggested question, and get a working token/cost comparison immediately — no GitHub API calls, no API keys.

| Demo | Language | Indexed files | Symbols |
|------|----------|--------------|---------|
| [dotenv](https://github.com/motdotla/dotenv) | JavaScript | 15 | 102 |
| [meow](https://github.com/sindresorhus/meow) | TypeScript | 24 | 63 |

To (re)generate the demo indexes from live repos:

```bash
npm run ingest:demo   # fetches via GitHub REST API, writes src/data/*.index.json
```

### Running locally

```bash
npm install
npm run dev
# http://localhost:3000
```

The token/cost comparison works **with no API key**. To get generated answers, set one LLM key in `.env.local` (copy `.env.example`): `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` or `GROQ_API_KEY`. If the LLM call fails or rate-limits, the comparison still renders — the metrics don't depend on the model call.

## How it works

### Phase 1 — Ingestion & indexing

- Parse a GitHub URL into owner/repo/ref.
- Fetch the file tree via `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/{sha}?recursive=1`, filter to source files (`.ts/.tsx/.js/.jsx/.py/.go`).
- Fetch individual files via `GET /repos/{owner}/{repo}/contents/{path}`.
- **Symbol extraction uses language-specific regex heuristics, not a full parser.** This is a deliberate, documented shortcut: web-tree-sitter (WASM) is heavier to make reliable in serverless, and the project's point is *measurement*, not perfect parsing. Caveats: nested closures are folded into their enclosing top-level declaration; anonymous/default exports are matched by the following declaration. This is a documented shortcut, not a hidden one.
- Build an **import graph** (which file imports which) by resolving relative module specifiers against known paths.
- Persist as JSON. Demos are committed statically; arbitrary repos are cached in memory for the instance lifetime.

**Hard caps** on arbitrary repos: reject anything over **~400 files** or **~5MB** of source with a clear error explaining why (a single serverless request must finish).

### Phase 2 — The two retrieval paths

**Naive:** score files by keyword overlap (question vs path + content), take top N, concatenate full contents up to a 24k token budget.

**Compressed:**
- Score **symbols** against the question (name 3×, signature 2×, body 1×).
- Take top-K symbols, pull their full source.
- Walk the import graph one hop out and include only **signatures/docstrings** for neighbors, not bodies.
- Include a compact **repo skeleton** (file tree + exported symbol names) for structural awareness.

Both produce a prompt string; tokens are counted with js-tiktoken. Costs use the pricing assumptions in `src/lib/cost.ts` (default Claude Sonnet $3/$15 per 1M tokens) — update freely.

### Phase 3 — Comparison UI

Single page. Demo chips + custom URL input, question box with suggested questions per demo, then a two-column result: strategy name, tokens, cost, latency, streamed answer, collapsible "show the context that was sent" panel, and a prominent delta readout.

## The honest eval

The eval set spans four question types across both demo repos — local definition, multi-hop data flow, dependency-aware (what breaks), and global (what does this repo do). Run it with `npm run eval` (token/cost runs with no key; add a key to also dump model answers for verdicts).

| # | repo | type | naive tok | comp tok | reduced | naive cost | comp cost | verdict |
|---|------|------|-----------|----------|---------|-----------|-----------|---------|
| 1 | dotenv | local | 15519 | 3818 | 75% | $0.05256 | $0.01745 | |
| 2 | dotenv | dependency | 9826 | 2372 | 76% | $0.03548 | $0.01312 | |
| 3 | dotenv | multi-hop | 15854 | 2185 | 86% | $0.05356 | $0.01256 | |
| 4 | dotenv | global | 86 | 520 | −505% | $0.00626 | $0.00756 | **worse** |
| 5 | meow | local | 9756 | 4774 | 51% | $0.03527 | $0.02032 | |
| 6 | meow | multi-hop | 8381 | 3659 | 56% | $0.03114 | $0.01698 | |
| 7 | meow | dependency | 9106 | 1989 | 78% | $0.03332 | $0.01197 | |
| 8 | meow | global | 86 | 559 | −550% | $0.00626 | $0.00768 | **worse** |

### Where compression loses

**Global questions ("what does this repo do?") are where the compressed path underperforms.** A broad question shares no keywords with the source, so keyword-overlap retrieval finds almost nothing: the naive path sends ~86 tokens (just the prompt boilerplate), while the compressed path always sends a repo skeleton, so it sends *more* tokens (~520–560) for no gain in relevance.

Two honest takeaways from this:

1. **Keyword-overlap retrieval collapses on broad questions** regardless of path — neither path builds a useful context for "what does this repo do?" because the words in the question don't appear in the code. This is the biggest gap in the current approach and would be where embeddings (an explicit non-goal) would help most.
2. **Compression isn't free on sparse matches.** When the naive path matches nothing, it sends near-nothing; the compressed path's mandatory skeleton makes it look worse on token count even though the skeletons were cheap to begin with. The metric that matters is *quality-per-token*, not raw tokens.

For the *local / multi-hop / dependency* types (rows 1–3, 5–7), compression cuts tokens 51–86% while the selected-symbol-plus-neighbor context is designed to preserve exactly the definitions and call sites those questions need. Verdicts on those rows should be filled after running with an LLM key (see Definition of done).

## Non-goals

- No auth, user accounts, or persistence of past runs.
- No chat history — one question, one comparison.
- No embeddings/vector search (listed as a clear follow-up).
- Only JS/TS/Python/Go indexed.

## Known shortcuts (documented, deliberate)

- **Regex symbol extraction** instead of web-tree-sitter (see Phase 1).
- **Keyword-overlap retrieval** instead of embeddings.
- **In-memory cache** for arbitrary repos (lost on cold start).
- **Cost assumptions** hardcoded in `src/lib/cost.ts`; latency numbers are from the actual model call where available.

## Deploying on Vercel

Push the repo, import into Vercel, add env vars. `maxDuration` is set to 120s in the API route; the true serverless ceiling for a plan is discovered empirically (see Phase 0 of the plan). The static demo indexes mean the deployed link works instantly with zero API keys.

# Assay
Status: archived
One-liner: An LLM evaluation harness with bootstrap confidence intervals and judge calibration.

Stack: Python, statistical evaluation
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Assay

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Most LLM eval reports a single accuracy number on a small test set and treats it as fact, when the sample is usually too small for the difference between two systems to mean anything. Assay adds bootstrap confidence intervals so a reported delta comes with an uncertainty range, and calibrates the judge model rather than assuming its scores are trustworthy. It's archived deliberately. The statistics were sound but the tool was too complex to actually use, which is a design failure regardless of how correct the internals are. The repo stays public because the underlying work is real, and the eval discipline from it now backs the portfolio assistant's grounding test suite.


## Anticipated questions
Q: Why keep an archived project on your portfolio?
A: Because the reason it was archived is a real engineering lesson — a correct tool nobody can use isn't a finished tool. Hiding it would just mean pretending every project landed.
