## README
# Assay

An eval harness for teams shipping LLM and agent features faster than they
can measure. Point a suite at a target, run graders, and get back a report
that answers three questions: did it pass, did it get worse than last time
beyond noise, and can you trust the grader that told you so.

Full spec lives in [`assay-prd.md`](./assay-prd.md),
[`assay-architecture.md`](./assay-architecture.md), and
[`assay-phases.md`](./assay-phases.md) — read those before making
architectural changes. [`CASE_STUDY.md`](./CASE_STUDY.md) is the
portfolio write-up (the problem, the two statistical choices, the
cost-control design); [`docs/launch-posts.md`](./docs/launch-posts.md)
has Show HN / LinkedIn / r/LocalLLaMA drafts.

## Stack

Next.js 15 (App Router, TypeScript), Supabase (Postgres + Auth), Upstash
(Redis + QStash), Drizzle ORM, Zod, Tailwind v4. See
`assay-architecture.md` §2 for the full rationale.

## Architecture

```text
                         ┌──────────────────────────────┐
   Browser ──────────────▶  Next.js on Vercel           │
   CI / curl ────────────▶                              │
                         │  /app          UI (RSC)      │
                         │  /api/v1/*     public API    │
                         │  /api/internal/worker        │
                         │  /api/internal/finalize      │
                         └───┬───────────┬──────────┬───┘
                             │           │          │
              enqueue chunks │           │ read/write
                             ▼           │          ▼
                    ┌────────────────┐   │   ┌──────────────────┐
                    │ Upstash QStash │   │   │ Supabase Postgres│
                    │  (push queue)  │   │   │  suites, cases,  │
                    └───────┬────────┘   │   │  runs, results,  │
                            │            │   │  labels, keys    │
             POST /worker   │            │   └──────────────────┘
                            ▼            ▼
                    ┌────────────────┐  ┌──────────────────────┐
                    │  Worker fn     │  │ Upstash Redis        │
                    │  runs 1 chunk  │  │ rate limits, quotas, │
                    └───────┬────────┘  │ budget, BYOK secrets │
                            │           └──────────────────────┘
                 target call│
                            ▼
              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
              │ Anthropic / Groq / OpenAI-   │
              │ compatible, or user endpoint │
              └──────────────────────────────┘
```

**Why the queue exists.** A suite run is not one request — it's N cases ×
K repeats × M graders, each of which can be a slow model call. The very
first version of this (Phase 1) ran everything inside one Server Action,
which works up to roughly 20 cases and then starts hitting serverless
function timeouts. Rather than paper over that with a bigger timeout, the
run is split at creation time into chunks of 5 cases, each pushed as its
own QStash message to `/api/internal/worker` — a normal, stateless HTTP
request Vercel can run as many of in parallel as needed, none of which has
to stay open for the whole run. Progress is a Redis counter incremented
per chunk, not a value derived from watching one long connection, so the
UI can poll it cheaply. A delayed `/api/internal/finalize` message and a
Vercel Cron sweep both exist as a safety net for the case a chunk never
reports back (crashed worker, dropped message) — a run should never get
stuck `running` forever with no way out.

**Deliberate rejections** — recorded because being able to explain a
rejected option is worth more in an interview than the option chosen
(`assay-architecture.md` §14):

- **Running evals inline in the request** — simplest, fails immediately
  past ~20 cases. Rejected at design time (Phase 1), not discovered at
  load time in production.
- **A separate Python worker on Railway/Fly** — a better eval-library
  ecosystem, but splits the stack, adds a second deploy target, and adds
  cold-start latency. The statistics needed (bootstrap CI, paired
  bootstrap, Spearman, quadratic-weighted kappa) are a few hundred lines
  total and not worth splitting the stack for.
- **Inngest instead of QStash** — nicer DX for step functions, heavier
  free-tier constraints for this shape of work. QStash's model of "HTTP
  push to your own endpoint" is the minimal fit for stateless chunked
  work.
- **SSE for progress** — familiar from earlier projects, but a persistent
  connection per report-page viewer is the wrong cost shape on
  serverless; a 2s Redis-backed poll costs nothing when nobody's watching.
- **Storing every generation for every run indefinitely** — the free
  Postgres tier would fill. Per-tier retention windows
  (`lib/limits/tiers.ts`, cleaned up by `/api/internal/cron/retention`)
  are a design feature, not a limitation to apologise for.

## Status

Building in phases per `assay-phases.md`. Currently:

- [x] **Phase 0 — Foundation.** Scaffold, schema, auth wiring, design
      tokens, test/CI setup.
- [x] **Phase 1 — Core eval engine.** All 10 deterministic graders, CSV/JSONL
      suite import, `static` target, synchronous run path (20-case cap),
      run report UI.
- [x] **Phase 2 — Async execution and model targets.** QStash-chunked worker
      with one inline retry + idempotent writes, `/api/internal/finalize`
      safety net, Redis-backed progress polling, `model` target (Ollama
      Cloud + Anthropic clients), `endpoint` target with the full
      `assertSafeUrl()` SSRF guard, three model-graded graders
      (`rubric_judge`, `faithfulness`, `answer_relevance`), stuck-run
      sweeper on Vercel Cron.
- [x] **Phase 3 — Variance, regression, and the report UI.** `lib/stats`
      (bootstrap CI, paired bootstrap, Spearman rank correlation), `k`
      repeats per case with per-case mean/stddev and the unstable-case
      flag, suite score always rendered as `score [lo – hi]`, per-tag
      slice table, a comparison view (verdict + effect size + sorted
      case-level deltas with side-by-side output diff), public share
      links at `/r/{shareId}`, and a `/methodology` page.
- [x] **Phase 4 — Public API, keys, and limits.** Hashed API keys with
      one-time reveal (`/dashboard/keys`), Bearer auth resolving key →
      owner → tier, `/api/v1/{suites,runs,usage}` + `/v1/runs/{id}/compare`
      (`?wait=true` long-polls), a fully unauthenticated + ephemeral
      `/v1/demo`, `@upstash/ratelimit` burst limits plus a separate
      runs/day quota (both `429` with `X-RateLimit-*`/`Retry-After`),
      pre-flight cost estimate (`402` before any provider call), a global
      daily budget with 80%/100% thresholds (dashboard banner + `503`),
      concurrency caps, BYOK (provider key encrypted into Redis for the
      run's duration only, deleted at finalize), `/docs` with a CI script,
      and a daily retention cron.
- [x] **Phase 5 — Judge calibration.** Stratified sampling of a judge's
      scored cases (spread across its own 1–5 range, not random), a
      keyboard-driven blind labelling flow (`1`–`5` to score, `→`/`Enter` to
      advance and reveal), quadratic-weighted Cohen's kappa + exact
      agreement % + Spearman + confusion matrix (`lib/stats/kappa.ts`),
      `graders.calibration` badge on every run report using that grader
      (`calibrated κ=0.71 (n=20, ...)` / `provisional (n<10)` /
      `uncalibrated`), kappa suppressed below 10 labels.
- [x] **Phase 6 — Launch polish.** Landing page with a live inline demo
      (`POST /v1/demo`, real request, no signup, no key, no cost) — 12
      cases, 3 deliberately wrong so the pass count is real, not rigged.
      3 seeded example suites (`lib/examples/suites.ts`: RAG faithfulness,
      structured extraction, adversarial-prompt safety) loadable from the
      dashboard's empty state. A suite detail page with run history
      (`/dashboard/suites/{id}`), needed so a suite can actually be found
      and re-run once the dashboard has more than one. Dynamic OG images
      on share links (`next/og`, suite name + score + CI). Lighthouse:
      100/100/100/100 on the landing page (accessibility was 93 before a
      contrast-token and missing-`<main>`-landmark fix, both driven by
      the audit rather than guessed at).

## Getting started

```bash
pnpm install
cp .env.example .env.local
pnpm dev
```

The app runs with nothing configured: the landing page works, and
`/dashboard` shows a setup notice instead of crashing. Each integration
below degrades gracefully until its env vars are set — fill them in as you
reach the phase that needs them.

### Supabase (auth + Postgres)

1. Create a project at [supabase.com](https://supabase.com).
2. Project Settings → API: copy the URL and `anon` key into
   `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL` / `NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`. Copy the
   `service_role` key into `SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY` (server-only, never
   exposed to the client).
3. Project Settings → Database → Connection string: copy the pooled
   ("Transaction mode") URL into `DATABASE_URL`.
4. Auth → Providers: confirm Email is enabled, and disable "Confirm email"
   if you want magic links to sign a new user in immediately.
5. Auth → URL Configuration: add `http://localhost:3000/auth/callback` (and
   your deployed origin's equivalent) as a redirect URL.
6. Apply the schema and RLS policies:

   ```bash
   pnpm db:migrate   # runs lib/db/migrations/*.sql against DATABASE_URL
   ```

   Then run [`lib/db/rls.sql`](./lib/db/rls.sql) once via the Supabase SQL
   editor (`pnpm db:migrate` only creates tables, not RLS policies). The
   migration was pre-generated with `pnpm db:generate`; re-run that
   yourself after changing `lib/db/schema.ts`. Drizzle treats `auth.users`
   as a read-only reference for foreign keys — it's declared in the schema
   but the generated SQL never creates or alters it, since Supabase already
   owns that table.

Signing in with a magic link creates a `projects` row for that user
(`app/auth/callback/route.ts` → `lib/db/queries.ts`).

### Upstash Redis + QStash (Phase 2)

Create a Redis database and a QStash instance at
[upstash.com](https://upstash.com); env var names are in `.env.example`.

For local dev, QStash needs a way to reach `/api/internal/worker` and
`/api/internal/finalize` without a public tunnel — run its local dev server
in a separate terminal:

```bash
npx @upstash/qstash-cli dev
```

It prints local `QSTASH_URL` / `QSTASH_TOKEN` / signing-key values; paste
those into `.env.local` in place of the real Upstash ones while developing
(standard signature verification, same code path as prod — just pointed at
localhost). Swap back to the real Upstash values for Preview/Prod.

(`@upstash/qstash` also ships its own auto-managed dev server, opted into
via `QSTASH_DEV=1` — see `instrumentation.ts`. Its auto-downloader currently
fails on Windows, so `qstash-cli` above is the reliable path there.)

### Model providers (Phase 2)

`model` targets and the three model-graded graders (`rubric_judge`,
`faithfulness`, `answer_relevance`) call out to a real provider:

- **Ollama Cloud** (`OLLAMA_API_KEY`, from
  [ollama.com/settings/keys](https://ollama.com/settings/keys)) — an
  OpenAI-compatible endpoint, model names use a `:cloud` suffix (e.g.
  `gpt-oss:120b-cloud`). These are reasoning models that spend real token
  budget on hidden reasoning before the visible answer — `lib/runs/judge.ts`
  gives judge calls generous `maxTokens` headroom for that reason.
- **Anthropic** (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) — supported by the same provider
  interface, not yet wired into local dev here.

Set `MOCK_PROVIDER=1` any time to fall back to deterministic fake outputs
instead — zero spend, zero flakiness. See `assay-architecture.md` §12.

### Vercel Cron (Phase 2)

`/api/internal/cron/sweep` finalizes runs stuck `queued`/`running` past a
10-minute wall-clock ceiling. `vercel.json` schedules it every 10 minutes;
set `CRON_SECRET` (any random string) in both `.env.local` and the Vercel
project's env vars — Vercel Cron sends it back as
`Authorization: Bearer <value>`.

### A note on `NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL` for local QStash testing

Use `http://127.0.0.1:3000`, not `http://localhost:3000` — the local
QStash dev server's own SSRF check resolves `localhost` and sometimes picks
the `::1` (IPv6) address, which it then rejects as a loopback destination.
`127.0.0.1` sidesteps the ambiguity.

### Public API, keys, and limits (Phase 4)

1. Sign in, go to `/dashboard/keys`, create a key (`free` or `byok` tier —
   there's no billing, so this is just which limits apply). The full key is
   shown once; only a hash and an 8-char prefix are stored.
2. `CRYPTO_KEK` (see above) must be set — every BYOK run and any `endpoint`
   target with custom headers needs it, and requests fail loudly without it.
3. `DAILY_BUDGET_CENTS` gates non-BYOK spend globally — see `/docs` and
   `assay-architecture.md` §8 for the two thresholds. `static`/`endpoint`
   targets never draw on it (no provider call to pay for); only a non-BYOK
   `model` target does.
4. Full endpoint list, curl examples, and a copy-paste CI script live at
   `/docs`. Tier limits (`lib/limits/tiers.ts`) are the single source of
   truth for case/grader/k/concurrency caps across both the API and, later,
   the dashboard UI.

Verified against the real pipeline: `POST /v1/suites` → `POST /v1/runs`
(both `static` and a real Ollama `model` target) → `?wait=true` → `/compare`
→ `/usage`, all through the actual HTTP routes, plus a BYOK run with a
deliberately wrong provider key (confirmed the override reaches the
provider call — Ollama returned a real `401`, not a silent fallback to the
platform key), the burst rate limit (`429` at request 61/min), the
anonymous demo's daily quota (`429` at request 4/day), and the budget gate
(`503` for a non-BYOK `model` run once the daily ceiling is crossed, static
targets unaffected).

### Judge calibration (Phase 5)

From a completed run's report, any model-graded grader (`rubric_judge`,
`faithfulness`, `answer_relevance`) shows a "Calibrate →" link next to its
row in the grader breakdown table, leading to
`/dashboard/runs/{runId}/calibrate/{graderId}`. It samples up to 20 of that
grader's scored cases — spread across the 1–5 range it actually produced,
not a random draw — and presents them one at a time: you see the case
input/output and pick a score with the `1`–`5` keys, then press `→` (or
`Enter`) to reveal the judge's own score/rationale for that same case and
advance. Once every sampled case is scored, the grader's calibration record
is written and a badge appears on every subsequent run report using that
grader.

Verified against the real pipeline: a real Ollama judge call graded 6 cases
built to span the full agreement spectrum (a clean match, a paraphrase, an
outright wrong answer, an off-topic answer, and one deliberately-wrong
answer), producing real 1–5 scores in `results.raw_score`; sampling,
blind-reveal, and relabelling-the-same-case-updates-not-duplicates were all
exercised against the live DB; and kappa came back correctly suppressed
(`null`) at n=6 (below the n=10 floor) while exact agreement and Spearman
still computed. `lib/stats/kappa.ts` is separately unit-tested against a
value cross-checked from scikit-learn's own `cohen_kappa_score` test suite.

### Launch polish (Phase 6)

- **Live inline demo** — the landing page's "Run this suite now" button
  calls the real, unauthenticated `POST /v1/demo` from the browser with a
  hardcoded 12-case suite (`app/(marketing)/inline-demo.tsx`). No suite,
  case, target, or run row is ever created for it — same ephemeral path
  `/v1/demo` has used since Phase 4.
- **Example suites** — `lib/examples/suites.ts` defines 3 suites (a
  faithfulness check using a real judge call, a JSON-schema extraction
  check, and an adversarial-prompt safety check), each with intentionally
  wrong outputs mixed in. `seedExampleSuites()` (`app/dashboard/actions.ts`)
  creates and runs all 3 for the signed-in user in one click from the
  dashboard's empty state; re-clicking is a no-op for suites already seeded
  (skips on the same unique-name constraint the "New suite" form's own
  duplicate-name handling relies on).
- **Suite detail page** (`/dashboard/suites/{id}`) — lists a suite's
  graders and every run of it, each linking to its report. This didn't
  exist before Phase 6: suites were listed on the dashboard but not
  clickable, so there was no way back to a suite's run history short of
  the API. Re-running an existing suite from the UI (rather than always
  creating a new one via "New suite") is still API-only — a gap, not a
  design choice; see `/docs`.
- **OG images** — `app/r/[shareId]/opengraph-image.tsx` renders a
  1200×630 PNG per share link via `next/og`, showing the suite name,
  cases-passed count, and suite score with its CI, read live from the run
  (`getRunSummaryByShareId` — a lighter query than the full report, since
  an OG image only needs the aggregate).

Verified against the real pipeline: the landing demo's "Run this suite
now" button was clicked live and returned 9/12 (the 3 deliberately-wrong
cases correctly flagged) — this caught a real bug first, where the demo's
grader was created with `isGate: false`, and case pass/fail is driven only
by *gate* graders, so every case silently showed "pass" regardless of its
score. The OG image route was hit directly against a real completed run
and rendered the actual score. All 3 example suites were seeded and run
end-to-end (including a real Ollama faithfulness call) with each
intentionally-wrong case confirmed to fail and each correct one to pass.

## Development

```bash
pnpm dev         # dev server
pnpm typecheck   # tsc --noEmit
```

# Sieve
Status: complete
One-liner: Two-stage invoice anomaly detection — unsupervised ensemble first, then a weakly-supervised classifier trained on its output.

Stack: Isolation Forest, LOF, LightGBM, SHAP, Streamlit, scikit-learn
Repository: https://github.com/SpandanNagale/Sieve

## Design rationale (why it was built this way)
Anomaly detection on invoices has no labels to start from, so stage one is unsupervised — Isolation Forest and LOF over invoice-level features (quantity, value, SKU count, customer behavior), with seasonal decomposition so that legitimate seasonal spikes don't get flagged as anomalies. Single detectors were rejected; each catches a different anomaly shape and neither covers the space alone. Stage two converts that into supervision cheaply: 150 hand-labeled invoices plus roughly 2000 weak labels derived from stage one, used to train a LightGBM classifier that outputs both a flag and a probability. SHAP explains each flag, because an anomaly score nobody can interpret doesn't get acted on. Evaluated with bootstrap confidence intervals on 500K+ transactions from the Online Retail dataset. Deliberately the non-LLM project in the portfolio — classical ML with evaluation rigor, to show the range isn't only agents.


## Anticipated questions
Q: Why weak supervision instead of labeling more data?
A: Hand-labeling invoices is slow and the class is rare, so a purely supervised approach would spend most of its labeling budget on normal invoices. Bootstrapping labels from the unsupervised stage concentrates the manual effort where it changes the model.


## Repository facts (from GitHub)
- Stars: 0
- Last commit: 2026-08-25T14:51:03Z
- GitHub description: Two-stage invoice anomaly detector: unsupervised outlier detection (IF + LOF + seasonal) → supervised refinement via weak supervision. Production-grade with rigorous evaluation.

## Languages (by bytes, from GitHub)
- Python: 46712

## README
# Sieve — Invoice Anomaly Detection

Two-stage anomaly detector on the [Online Retail dataset](https://archive.ics.uci.edu/dataset/352/online+retail) (~540K UK e-commerce transactions, Dec 2010–Dec 2011): unsupervised detection (Isolation Forest + LOF + seasonal residuals) feeding a weakly-supervised LightGBM classifier.

## Setup

```
python -m venv .venv
./.venv/Scripts/pip install -r requirements.txt
```

The raw dataset is already downloaded to `data/raw/online_retail.xlsx` (from UCI's public mirror — no Kaggle account needed).

## Pipeline

```
# Stage 1: clean data, engineer features, run the 3 unsupervised detectors,
# export the top 150 highest-scored invoices for hand labeling.
./.venv/Scripts/python run_pipeline.py stage1

# Label those 150 invoices yourself (genuine_error / business_event / normal_variance).
./.venv/Scripts/python -m streamlit run labeling_app/label_app.py

# Stage 3: build the hand+weak+negative training set, train the weighted
# LightGBM classifier, 5-fold CV on the hand-labeled set, compare against
# the Isolation-Forest-alone and unweighted-RandomForest baselines, SHAP plot.
./.venv/Scripts/python run_pipeline.py stage3

# Stage 4: upload a fresh invoice CSV and audit it.
./.venv/Scripts/python -m streamlit run dashboard/app.py
```

`run_pipeline.py all` runs stage1 then stage3 back to back (only useful once you already have hand labels).

## Layout

- `src/sieve/data.py` — load raw xlsx/csv, drop cancellations/returns, aggregate transactions to invoice level.
- `src/sieve/features.py` — per-customer stats and per-invoice anomaly features (z-scores, days-since-last-order, weekly frequency, trend).
- `src/sieve/stage1_unsupervised.py` — Isolation Forest, LOF, and a seasonal-residual detector; also the fit/score split used to serve genuinely new invoices in the dashboard without refitting on every small upload.
- `src/sieve/stage2_labeling.py` — exports invoices for hand labeling, derives weak labels from detector-agreement patterns, assembles the Stage 3 training set.
- `src/sieve/stage3_supervised.py` — weighted LightGBM binary (`is_anomaly`) and multiclass models, 5-fold CV on hand labels, baseline comparisons.
- `src/sieve/evaluate.py` — bootstrap CIs, confusion matrix plotting.
- `src/sieve/shap_analysis.py` — SHAP summary plot for the binary model.
- `labeling_app/label_app.py` — Streamlit tool for Stage 2 hand labeling.
- `dashboard/app.py` — Streamlit audit dashboard for Stage 4, with a human-review logging form.

## Notes on deviations from a literal reading of the spec

- No `total_weight` / shipping-weight column exists in this dataset, so the Isolation Forest runs on `[Quantity, InvoiceValue, num_skus]` only.
- The spec's seasonal decomposition is per outlet × SKU; that needs transaction-level series. Invoices are already aggregated to one row per invoice by the time Stage 1 runs, so the seasonal detector instead decomposes each **customer's** weekly order-value total (STL where there's ≥32 weeks of history, a rolling mean/std z-score fallback otherwise).
- `is_anomaly` (the Stage 3 binary target) is 1 for both `genuine_error` and `business_event`, 0 for `normal_variance` — the classifier's job is filtering out false positives, not just detecting magnitude.
- The RandomForest baseline uses the same features and training pool as the LightGBM model but uniform sample weights, isolating what the hand+weak-label weighting scheme buys you.
